strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful VFI problem: consistency across interpolated frames and temporal chunks. Combining video-conditioned diffusion forcing with independently generated anchor chunks and bridge chunks is a plausible approach to limiting recursive error propagation.

Table 1 shows consistent FVD improvements over the evaluated baselines across all four settings. For example, LDF-VFI achieves 26.26 versus BiM-VFI’s 38.26 on SNU-FILM-16× and 51.41 versus 69.83 on XTest-16×. These are worthwhile video-level perceptual gains even without uniformly superior frame-level accuracy.

The ablations provide useful component-level evidence. With the unconditional decoder held fixed, skip-concatenate sampling reduces average FVD from 22.67 to 17.05. Adding the conditional decoder reduces average LPIPS from 0.060 to 0.051. Table 3 also supports nearest-neighbor conditioning over zero padding for keyframe reconstruction.

The architecture combines practical mechanisms for processing larger videos, including spatially local attention, tiled VAE processing, and fixed temporal windows. Figure 5 illustrates reduced deformation and blur in challenging examples, and the paper supplies several concrete training and inference hyperparameters.
weaknesses: The central claim of stable generation over arbitrarily long sequences is insufficiently tested. No evaluation reports quality versus sequence length or temporal position, errors at chunk boundaries, or the durations actually evaluated. Aggregate FVD measures distributional video quality and cannot by itself establish that temporal drift is bounded. The sampling design plausibly breaks recursive dependencies, but the stronger claim of duration-independent error is not demonstrated.

The comparisons do not adequately separate the proposed temporal modeling contribution from the benefits of a pretrained video diffusion model. All four quantitative baselines are flow-based, although the paper discusses several diffusion-based VFI methods. There is also no matched ablation against independently generated chunks or a frame-pair version of the same backbone. Consequently, the results establish advantages over the listed systems but leave the source of those advantages and competitiveness with the closest generative approaches unresolved.

The newly constructed benchmarks are underspecified in ways that materially affect interpretation and reproducibility. The paper does not give the evaluated video counts, sequence lengths, exact source-video selection, or FVD clip sampling and preprocessing protocol. It is also unclear whether observed input frames are included in LPIPS or replaced with their originals. Section 4.3 discusses SNU-FILM-hard, SNU-FILM-extreme, and XTest-4K, whereas Table 1 reports interpolation factors without corresponding split or resolution breakdowns.

The efficiency and resolution-scalability claims exceed the evidence. Local attention reduces spatial attention complexity, but computation still grows with the number of spatial tokens; it does not decouple cost from resolution as claimed. The reported ability to run 4K inference on two 80GB GPUs is useful feasibility evidence, but no runtime, peak-memory measurements, scaling curves, or full-attention comparison establish practical efficiency. The spatial attention window configuration and exact Wan2.1 model variant are also unspecified.

Claims of superior per-frame quality require qualification. LDF-VFI has the best LPIPS in only one of four Table 1 settings; on XTest-16×, its 0.071 is worse than BiM-VFI’s 0.055. This does not negate the FVD gains, but supports a fidelity–video-quality tradeoff rather than uniform superiority. Similarly, the conditional decoder slightly worsens FVD at SNU-FILM-8×, from 14.55 to 15.01.

There is a correctable technical inconsistency in Section 3.1: the stated path x_t = (1−t)x_1 + tx_0 places noise at t=0 and data at t=1, consistent with the target velocity x_0−x_1, but inference is described as integrating from t=1 to t=0. This leaves the written sampling specification inconsistent. This issue alone would not determine rejection; the recommendation primarily reflects the missing evidence for long-sequence stability and the insufficiently specified, unmatched evaluation.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful VFI problem: maintaining consistency across interpolated frames and temporal chunks. Combining chunk-level diffusion forcing with independently generated anchor chunks and conditioned bridging chunks is a plausible, useful design.

Table 1 reports the best FVD across all four settings. Against BiM-VFI, FVD improves from 38.26 to 26.26 on SNU-FILM-16× and from 69.83 to 51.41 on XTest-16×. These results support a contribution even though LPIPS is not consistently best.

The component ablations provide useful evidence. With the same unconditional decoder, skip-concatenate sampling reduces average FVD from 22.67 to 17.05. Adding the conditional decoder improves average LPIPS from 0.060 to 0.051. Table 3 also supports nearest-neighbor conditioning over zero padding for keyframe reconstruction.

The architecture is reasonably well motivated and illustrated. Figure 5 shows examples with fewer visible interpolation artifacts, and reported 4K inference demonstrates practical feasibility beyond the 512×512 training crops.
weaknesses: The central claim of sustained long-video stability is insufficiently tested. The manuscript does not report evaluated sequence lengths, quality versus temporal position or duration, or errors specifically at chunk boundaries. Aggregate FVD measures distributional video quality and does not isolate accumulated drift. Table 2 supports a better sampling order, but does not establish the stronger claim that error remains constant regardless of video duration. An independent-chunk baseline is also missing, leaving the benefit of bridging over simple resets unclear.

The new evaluation protocol is materially underspecified. Section 4.2 does not provide the main benchmarks' video counts, exact source-sequence selection, clip lengths, or FVD extraction and aggregation protocol. It is also unclear whether LPIPS includes observed frames and whether these are reconstructed or copied. These details matter for interpreting the reported improvements and reproducing the proposed benchmarks.

Comparisons omit the diffusion-based VFI methods that motivate the paper, including LDMVFI, EDEN, and VIDIM. All evaluated competitors are frame-pair methods, whereas LDF-VFI uses broader context and a pretrained Wan backbone. This comparison demonstrates useful performance against those systems, but does not establish superiority over relevant generative approaches or isolate the contribution of holistic modeling from pretraining and model capacity.

The efficiency claims exceed the evidence. Local attention reduces attention complexity, but total computation still grows with spatial resolution; it does not decouple computational cost from image resolution as claimed. The reported requirement of two 80GB GPUs establishes 4K feasibility, while missing runtime, measured peak memory, model size, and resolution-scaling comparisons prevent assessment of the claimed efficiency.

Several correctable technical and reporting issues reduce clarity and reproducibility. Section 3.1 defines the interpolation path as noise at t=0 and data at t=1, but specifies sampling from t=1 to t=0 with the corresponding forward velocity. The exact Wan checkpoint and spatial attention window are unspecified. Section 4.3 discusses hard/extreme splits that are not the labels reported in Table 1, and the abstract's claim of superior per-frame quality needs qualification: RIFE has better LPIPS at SNU-FILM-4×, and BiM-VFI at SNU-FILM-16× and XTest-16×. These issues alone would not determine rejection; the weak-reject recommendation primarily reflects the gaps in validating long-term stability and establishing a reproducible, relevant comparison.

strengths: The paper addresses an important VFI limitation: independently interpolating adjacent frame pairs does not explicitly coordinate motion across a longer sequence. Combining chunk-level diffusion forcing with video conditioning is a plausible and potentially useful approach.

Skip-concatenate sampling is a concrete methodological contribution. Generating independent anchor chunks and then bridging them offers a sensible way to interrupt autoregressive error propagation. Table 2 supports its benefit: with the same unconditional decoder, average FVD improves from 22.67 to 17.05, while LPIPS improves slightly.

Table 1 reports the best FVD among the evaluated methods across all four settings, including improvements over BiM-VFI from 38.26 to 26.26 on SNU-FILM-16× and from 69.83 to 51.41 on XTest-16×. These are meaningful positive results even though the method does not consistently lead on LPIPS.

The conditioning choices have empirical support. Adding the conditional decoder reduces average LPIPS from 0.060 to 0.051, and nearest-neighbor input filling improves keyframe reconstruction over zero padding. Figure 5 also illustrates sharper reconstructions in difficult motion examples.
weaknesses: The central claim of stable long-video generation is insufficiently established. The paper does not report evaluation sequence-length distributions, quality versus rollout position or duration, or measurements around chunk boundaries. Aggregate FVD captures broader distributional differences and does not specifically demonstrate bounded error accumulation or seamless inter-chunk motion. Table 2 supports the proposed ordering, but an independent-chunk baseline is also needed to establish the value of bridging over simply resetting generation.

The comparative evidence does not establish the claimed advance over diffusion-based VFI. All four evaluated baselines are flow-based, despite the manuscript discussing LDMVFI, EDEN, MADiff, LBBDM, and VIDIM. There is also no controlled comparison restricting the proposed model's temporal context, so the effects of holistic modeling are not separated from those of the pretrained Wan backbone and generative architecture. This is a material gap in positioning the contribution, rather than merely a request for more benchmarks.

The newly constructed benchmarks are not specified sufficiently for reproduction or confident interpretation. Section 4.2 omits exact sequence selection, counts and lengths, while FVD clip extraction, preprocessing, and sample counts are unspecified. It is also unclear whether observed frames enter the reported metrics and whether they are copied or reconstructed. These details matter particularly because FVD is the main evidence for superiority. The actual fidelity results are mixed: XTest LPIPS is 0.071 versus BiM-VFI's 0.055.

The efficiency claims exceed the evidence. Local attention avoids quadratic spatial attention, but total computation still grows with spatial token count; it does not decouple computation from resolution as claimed. Reporting that 4K inference fits across two 80GB GPUs demonstrates feasibility, not efficiency. Runtime, peak memory, scaling measurements, and an attention ablation are absent, leaving practical usefulness and the cost of the quality gains unclear.

Several technical and reporting details need correction or clarification. Section 3.1 defines a noise-to-data path with velocity x0−x1 but then describes integrating from t=1 to 0, reversing the stated convention. The precise Wan model variant and spatial attention window are unspecified. Section 4.3 refers to hard/extreme splits that do not match Table 1's labels. These are individually correctable issues; my weak-reject recommendation is driven primarily by the missing evidence for long-range stability and comparative contribution, together with the underspecified evaluation protocol.

strengths: The paper makes a useful contribution to sequence-level VFI: chunk-level diffusion forcing and skip-concatenate sampling combine joint interpolation with bounded temporal context. The sampling strategy is a concrete, well-motivated adaptation to strongly conditioned video generation.

Tables 1–2 report the best FVD among evaluated methods in all four settings. Particularly meaningful gains occur on SNU-FILM-16× (26.26 versus 38.26 for BiM-VFI) and X4K-16× (51.41 versus 69.83), while frame-level perceptual quality remains competitive.

The component ablations provide credible support: skip-concatenate sampling reduces average FVD from 22.67 to 17.05 with the same unconditional decoder, and conditional decoding subsequently improves average LPIPS from 0.060 to 0.051. Figure 6 also illustrates reduced chunk-boundary discontinuities.

Training at 512×512 and demonstrating inference at 4K is practically relevant. Table 5 supports sparse attention through substantial improvements over full attention in both runtime and high-resolution quality.
The architecture and training recipe are generally understandable. Taken together, the supported temporal-quality gains and useful system design favor acceptance despite the limitations below.
weaknesses: The claim of constant error accumulation and temporal stability for arbitrarily long videos exceeds the evidence. Independent skip chunks break recursive dependence, but do not guarantee consistent motion across independently generated anchors. Figure 6 covers roughly 300 frames, and no quantitative quality-versus-duration analysis establishes sustained long-video behavior.

The new benchmark protocols are insufficiently specified: test-video counts, sequence lengths, exact source selection, and FVD clip extraction and preprocessing are missing. Whether observed frames are included in frame-level metrics is also unclear. These omissions materially affect reproducibility and interpretation of the central FVD results; no uncertainty estimates are reported.

The results support improved FVD more strongly than general superiority in fidelity or motion accuracy. On X4K, BiM-VFI outperforms LDF-VFI on LPIPS, VFIPS, and FloLPIPS; on SNU-FILM-4×, several baselines also provide better frame-level scores. FVD alone does not isolate temporal consistency or establish faithful motion reconstruction.

Attribution of the overall advantage to holistic modeling remains incomplete. Comparisons combine a pretrained Wan backbone, different training resources, broader temporal context, and architectural changes. A matched pairwise or independent-chunk baseline evaluated quantitatively would better isolate the benefit; the non-AR comparison is only illustrated in Figure 6.

Resolution scalability comes with substantial resource costs. Table 4 reports 16.3 seconds per 4K frame using four H100 GPUs at 16 steps, versus 1.4 seconds for BiM-VFI on one GPU. Sparse attention improves efficiency relative to full attention, but practical efficiency relative to established VFI methods remains limited.

Important implementation details remain unspecified, including the Wan model variant, exact sparse-attention window configuration, and treatment of observed frames in the final output. The abstract's code-availability statement has no link. The claimed support for arbitrary non-integer interpolation ratios is also not evaluated.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful limitation of pairwise video frame interpolation: temporal consistency across successive predictions. Joint chunk generation with skip-concatenate sampling is a coherent, potentially useful contribution. The supported improvements favor weak acceptance, despite reservations about the broader claims.

The strongest empirical result is consistent FVD improvement across all four benchmark settings. On SNU-FILM-16×, FVD decreases from the strongest listed baseline's 38.26 to 26.26; on X4K-16×, it decreases from 69.83 to 51.41. These results support the value of sequence-level modeling without requiring superiority on every metric.

Table 3 provides a useful controlled ablation: changing causal sampling to skip-concatenate with the same unconditional decoder reduces average FVD from 22.67 to 17.05. Adding the conditional decoder reduces average LPIPS from 0.060 to 0.051. Figure 6 supplies complementary evidence of reduced chunk-boundary discontinuities.

The scalability design has experimental support. Table 5 shows substantially better 4K generalization and lower runtime with sparse attention than full attention under matched training and sampling settings. The supplementary chunk-length comparison also supports the benefit of broader temporal context. Training losses, optimization settings, and sampling parameters are described reasonably clearly.
weaknesses: The claim of constant error accumulation regardless of video duration is stronger than the evidence. Independent skip chunks break recursive dependencies, but this does not establish uniformly accurate or globally coherent predictions. Figure 6 illustrates one sequence, while Table 3 reports aggregate metrics; neither measures error versus rollout duration over a dataset. The demonstrated contribution is improved finite-window consistency, rather than a validated guarantee for arbitrarily long videos.

The new benchmark protocols are insufficiently specified for confident reproduction. The manuscript does not clearly report the full test-set sizes, sequence-length distributions, FVD clip extraction and preprocessing, or whether observed frames are included in scoring or replaced with original inputs. These omissions matter particularly because FVD is the principal metric showing consistent superiority. No uncertainty estimates are reported.

The results establish a metric tradeoff rather than uniformly superior reconstruction. On X4K-16×, BiM-VFI outperforms LDF-VFI on LPIPS (0.055 versus 0.071), VFIPS (-69.98 versus -64.80), and FloLPIPS (0.065 versus 0.082). EDEN also has better LPIPS and FloLPIPS on SNU-FILM-4×. FVD captures distributional video similarity and does not alone demonstrate accurate motion or temporal correspondence, so the abstract's broad superiority claims need qualification.

The novelty lies mainly in the VFI-specific integration and sampling order: diffusion forcing, the pretrained Wan backbone, tiled VAEs, local attention, and ControlNet-style conditioning are established ingredients. Although the sampling ablation is persuasive, there is no matched pairwise-versus-video-context experiment using the same pretrained backbone and training data. Consequently, comparisons with external baselines do not isolate how much improvement comes from the proposed formulation versus pretraining and model capacity.

Practical efficiency remains limited. The main 4K configuration takes 16.3 seconds per generated frame across four H100 GPUs, versus 1.4 seconds for BiM-VFI on one GPU. Even the two-step configuration uses four GPUs. This demonstrates feasibility and an improvement over full attention, but not broadly inexpensive 4K interpolation.

Several implementation details remain unclear, including the exact Wan model variant, spatial attention neighborhood, and boundary handling during skip-concatenate inference. The abstract's code-availability sentence has no link. These are reproducibility and presentation deficiencies; they do not invalidate the reported component gains, but they increase the effort required to verify them.

strengths: The paper presents a coherent and useful approach to sequence-level video frame interpolation. Chunk-level diffusion forcing, independent skip chunks, and bidirectionally conditioned bridging chunks provide a plausible mechanism for reducing error propagation while preserving continuity. The supported methodological contribution and empirical gains favor acceptance.

Temporal-quality improvements are consistent across the evaluated settings. LDF-VFI achieves the best reported FVD on all four benchmark configurations, including 26.26 versus 38.26 for the strongest baseline on SNU-FILM-16× and 51.41 versus 69.83 on X4K-16×. Improvements in FloLPIPS at SNU-FILM-8× and 16× provide additional evidence beyond FVD.

The ablations substantiate several design choices. With the decoder held fixed, skip-concatenate sampling reduces average FVD from 22.67 to 17.05; conditional decoding subsequently improves average LPIPS from 0.060 to 0.051. Figure 6 illustrates reduced chunk-boundary discontinuities, and the supplementary chunk-length experiment supports the usefulness of broader temporal context.

Resolution generalization is a valuable practical contribution. Training at 512×512 and evaluating at 4K demonstrates meaningful scalability, while Table 5 directly supports sparse attention over full attention under the reported training budget. The paper also reports sampling-step tradeoffs rather than presenting quality without computational context.
weaknesses: The central claim of duration-independent error control is stronger than the evidence. Table 3 reports aggregate quality, while Figure 6 compares against independent chunks rather than tracking causal-AR degradation over increasing sequence lengths. Independent skip chunks limit dependency chains, but this alone does not establish uniformly bounded perceptual error or long-range consistency. A duration-stratified evaluation is missing.

The new benchmark protocols are insufficiently specified for reproducing the principal results. The manuscript does not clearly report test-video counts and duration distributions, exact source-video selection, or the temporal sampling and preprocessing used for FVD. Whether observed input frames are included in quality metrics or replaced with originals is also unclear. These details matter particularly because the strongest overall advantage is in FVD; uncertainty across stochastic runs is not reported.

Claims of superior per-frame quality need qualification. EDEN has better LPIPS on SNU-FILM-4× and 8×, while BiM-VFI outperforms LDF-VFI on X4K LPIPS, VFIPS, and FloLPIPS (0.055 versus 0.071, -69.98 versus -64.80, and 0.065 versus 0.082). The evidence supports a favorable temporal-quality tradeoff, rather than uniformly superior interpolation fidelity.

The efficiency benefit is relative to full-attention diffusion, not to established VFI systems. At 16 sampling steps, SNU-FILM inference takes 3.36 seconds per frame versus 0.15 for BiM-VFI; 4K inference takes 16.3 seconds per frame using four H100 GPUs versus 1.4 seconds on one GPU. Even two-step 4K inference uses four GPUs. This substantially limits deployment usefulness despite the demonstrated resolution scalability.

The contribution primarily combines established diffusion forcing, pretrained video generation, local attention, and conditional decoding, with skip-concatenate sampling as the clearest distinctive element. Comparisons against pairwise systems do not fully separate the benefits of additional temporal context from those of WAN pretraining and model capacity. Reproduction is further hindered by the unspecified WAN model variant and attention-window configuration, and the manuscript's code-availability statement contains no link.
